parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need this new service to do for you?

I plan and run our flights, and as the licensed person responsible for each flight, I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones. Our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, but I want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts.
ASK technician: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need this new service to do for you?

I keep the drones and charging equipment in working order for my company. My tasks include adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can also ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after. I do not know what I need this new service to do for me.
ASK desk: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need this new service to do for you?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
ASK dispatcher: Can you walk me through the entire lifecycle of a job and a flight, from creation to completion or cancellation?

Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, such as the load being ready or not, the drone reaching the points of its job, and the drone arriving. People and devices outside our company report these things, and I can call off a flight.
ASK dispatcher: What details define a job (both delivery and inspection), and what rules must be checked when you assign a drone, choose a route, and sign off a flight?
